source.title: Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design
source.authors: Michal Derezinski; Feynman T. Liang; Michael W. Mahoney

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes double descent in linear regression using exact surrogate-design formulas and empirical estimates under i.i.d. Gaussian designs, rather than reproducing deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports MSE curves while varying sample size and feature dimension. Results on double descent cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The paper describes Figure 1's double-descent peak, but gives plotted rather than tabulated MSE values.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact MSE expressions for the minimum-norm linear estimator under a surrogate design. It sweeps sample size n (Fig 1a, d=100), with empirical i.i.d. Gaussian checks, and feature dimension d (Fig 2, n=100). Both sweeps show a peak at n=d with descent on either side. This is a different method (exact theory on linear regression) aimed at the same double-descent question.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors give exact non-asymptotic MSE for the Moore-Penrose estimator under a DPP surrogate design that reproduces double descent as n crosses d. They show the surrogate is asymptotically consistent with i.i.d. designs (Theorem 3, conjectured O(1/d) rate). They also show that min-norm interpolation equals population ridge regression in expectation.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives exact results for a DPP-based surrogate random design and compares them with empirical standard i.i.d. Gaussian linear-regression estimates; it does not use deep-network training.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that covariance spectral decay changes the shape of the underdetermined-regime curve; with rapid decay, the MSE can have a local optimum for n < d.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the surrogate design, the expected min-norm estimator for n<d equals the population ridge solution, with λn set so that the ridge effective dimension equals n. Figure 1b shows shrinkage matching this for i.i.d. Gaussians.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-parameterized min-norm interpolation acts as implicit ridge regularization whose strength is set by the degree of over-parameterization.

fits_no_version.finding: Surrogate MSE expressions converge to i.i.d. MSE asymptotically (Theorem 3). Empirical discrepancies decay at O(1/d) (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: none (methodological validity of the surrogate design)

record.problems: The plotted MSE values are not tabulated. The exact non-asymptotic expressions apply to a surrogate, non-i.i.d. design; the i.i.d. comparison is empirical. The study evaluates linear regression rather than deep networks or a broad range of model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported MSE rows omitted. The bias and variance discrepancy plots in Figure 4 concern approximation error between designs, not the test-error curve named by the claim.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied, and model size is varied only as the linear feature dimension.
Training time or epochs are not studied.
Only linear regression with Gaussian-type designs is tested; deep networks and other model classes are not.
Only one model class (min-norm linear regression) is tested. The d sweep is theory-only under the surrogate design, with no empirical i.i.d. check.
Ridge effective dimension appears as the implicit regularization parameter, but no test shows it predicts peak location across axes.
There is no label-noise or regularization sweep, and multiple peaks and optimal ridge are not examined.
Complexity is not recounted via an effective number of parameters to see whether the curve turns into a U-shape.

missing.what: The exact peak value at n=d is MSE = σ²tr(Σ⁻¹) = 100 for all κ, since Σ is scaled so that tr(Σ⁻¹)=d. This gives a numeric value for the peak that the rows lack.

record.verdict_notes: The MSE here is parameter error E||ŵ−w*||², which equals prediction risk only for isotropic Σ. This should be kept in mind when comparing with test-error studies. The paper analyzes a phenomenon defined by the original sources but is not itself an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines linear regression, not deep networks.
It does not vary training epochs or report epoch-wise test error.
The sample-size sweep is for linear regression; it does not test deep networks or other model classes.
The tested model class is linear regression; other model classes are not evaluated.
The study relates sample size to ridge effective dimension, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
There is no sweep of label noise or regularization, nor a test of multiple peaks or their disappearance under optimal regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that transforms the curve into an ordinary U-shape.

rows.note: The text says the plotted MSE has a double-descent peak at n = d. Exact curve values are not tabulated.
rows.check: This sweep varies samples with capacity fixed, so it bears on V3 (more data hurts near n=d), not on V4's capacity axis. Remove the V4 link. For isotropic Σ, Theorem 1 gives MSE = σ²n/(d−n) + ||w*||²(d−n)/d for n<d, which rises with n up to the threshold.
